newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin no longer spooks Russian markets.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin no longer spooks Russian markets.

text.p: Russia's young markets, which used to tremble when President Boris Yeltsin sneezed, have learnt to live with bad news about his health, financial analysts said on Thursday.
"The market is now used to the fact that Yeltsin can be ill and the economy can still function," said Roland Nash, chief economist at Renaissance Capital investment bank.
"There is a renewed faith in Russia that we really have not seen for a long time."
Yeltsin, whose health problems sent the equities market into a slide last autumn in the run-up to his heart surgery in November, went into hospital late on Wednesday with pneumonia.

Top Russian shares, which have been in a rally testing historic highs, lost about 5-10 percent at the opening on Thursday but began recovering within minutes and found support at levels near Wednesday's close.
Mosenergo utility, a bellwether of the market, had recovered by mid-afternoon to $1.27 from a morning low of $1.14 and $1.33 on Wednesday. It traded at under one dollar on December 27.
Many shares had gained on the previous close by afternoon.
Russian MinFin bonds also recovered after an initial fall, while prices on domestic Treasury bills firmed as investors scrambled for paper after an oversubscribed auction on Wednesday, dealers said.
T-bill dealers acknowledged that the Yeltsin news could worry some foreign investors but said prices were rising on market fundamentals.

The rouble, which is strictly controlled by the central bank, has traditionally not reacted to political news, although it would be vulnerable to a heavy outflow of foreign investment from the T-bill market.
Increased competition for a limited number of shares and T-bills has made investors, many experienced in last autumn's health crisis, less willing to wait to invest, analysts said.
Equity turnover on the Russian Trading System hit a historic high of $55 million on Wednesday as new investors and new funds bid up share prices.

If Yeltsin's pneumonia is over in a couple of weeks as doctors say, it will slow not stop a rally which has seen equity prices rise about 15 percent this year, said Christopher Granville, head of research at United City Bank.
"New allocations by Western institutions are based on a global assessment of Russia, and an ailing president is part of that picture," he said.
"It is going to take much more dramatic news to dramatically change the picture."
He predicted the market would appreciate by a total 25 percent by the end of February, a gain he said could have made by the end of January without the Yeltsin health news.
T-bill yields are also broadly expected to decline.
Russia is attracting attention because it is one of the best buys in an increasingly expensive global investment climate, said James Fenkner, chief of research at CentreInvest Securities.
"You have to go out further on the risk curve to get anywhere," he said, pointing to high prices in developed markets such as the United States.
Russian equities are set to double their value this year, said Gavin Rankin, director of research at Moscow's Troika-Dialog bank.
"Yeltsin's health is not enough to knock a bull off its feet," he said.
